title: Evals in AI: A Deep Dive — Tejas Kumar, IBM
talk_summary: Tejas Kumar (IBM) frames evals as 'fuzzy unit tests' for non-deterministic systems and walks through building an LLM-judge eval pipeline live: golden dataset, judge agreement training, CI agreement gate, and RAG-injected policy. He documents concrete judge biases (position, sycophancy, self-preference, verbosity) and a cheap-to-expensive escalation ladder for eval cost.

takeaways.technique: Train the LLM judge against a human-scored golden set and gate on agreement rate, not raw pass/fail
takeaways.what_they_do: Keep a set of ~30 scenario/answer/human-verdict examples; strip the verdict, have the judge score, compute agreement; iterate by adding missing policy context until agreement hits 80-85%; fail CI only when agreement drops below threshold (and flag 100% as overfit).
takeaways.evidence_quote: only fail the test if human AI agreement drops below, I don't know, 80%. Right? Otherwise, pass.
takeaways.numbers: 80-85% agreement target; 30-example seed set; 100% agreement treated as overfit red flag

takeaways.what_they_do: Names four biases with mechanisms: position bias (swap order to detect), sycophancy (judge picks the nicer answer over policy-correct), self-preference (judge favors its own model family's output), verbosity (longer answers win). Mitigations: pointwise instead of pairwise, different model family for judge, explicit 'policy is non-negotiable no matter how nice the user is' instructions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: your judge needs to be a different model family from the rest of your corpus if you're generating text
takeaways.numbers: pairwise 39% more vulnerable to attack than pointwise

takeaways.what_they_do: Escalate only as needed: deterministic unit tests first, then regex/pattern matching, then trace inspection (tool calls as JSON, call counts, latencies), and only then an LLM judge starting with the cheapest capable model.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you want to go as cheap as possible... start with actual deterministic tests... eventually you'll come to a place where you need to use a judge and then you start with the cheapest model

takeaways.technique: Inject the authoritative policy into the judge prompt via RAG, shared with the production agent
takeaways.what_they_do: Hardcoded policy first, then moved it to a retrieval source (OpenRAG) queried by both the production agent and the judge so they share one source of truth; adding the missing policy clause fixed the residual disagreements.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the production LLM agent and the judge should share the same policy... the policy must be one to one
takeaways.numbers: agreement went from failing (>5 of 30) to 27/30 passing after policy injection + model bump

takeaways.technique: Escalate model only after context is maxed out
takeaways.what_they_do: When the cheap judge (GPT-3.5) still disagreed after policy injection, they bumped to a mid-tier model (4o-mini) and got consistent, correctly-cased verdicts — but only after exhausting prompt/context fixes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we've maxed out what we can do we've given context... now is a good time to think about let's use a higher quality model

takeaways.technique: Eval suite as a CI quality gate with a living dataset
takeaways.what_they_do: Run the eval suite in CI; red if agreement below threshold; in production, skim real traffic, have humans score samples, and feed them back into the golden set so the judge stays current; use synthetic/adversarial generation to grow the set without waiting for customers.
takeaways.evidence_quote: run my evals on CI... if my judge agrees with me less than the threshold... then I don't ship
